## Quotable phrasings (sorted by approximate impact)

The top tier — phrases that did the heaviest lifting and are most transferable to other reps:

1. **"You're taking 25% out of what you weren't going to get anything from before."** — re-frames the revenue split as a success fee, neutralises the entire "25% too high" objection territory.
2. **"It works on a ratchet. Year one you baseline. Year two it goes up — boom, you get credited. Year three you lose something, no penalty. You only get credited when you beat the previous high."** — the single most-repeated explanation, landed every time.
3. **"We don't do trees. It's nothing to do with trees. It's to do with your soil."** — kills the lock-up-the-land conflation in one sentence.
4. **"Our contract basically boils down to: make a commitment to be better, make a commitment to keep your land in the agricultural system for 25 years."** — reduces the 25-year fear to two clauses.
5. **"It only becomes a problem if you've been making money doing it. If you've been making credits, why would they throw away a revenue stream?"** — defuses property-sale objection by inverting the frame.
6. **"AgriProve is basically the verification machine. They're like the accountants kind of for soil carbon."** — the cleanest single-sentence positioning of the company.
7. **"If we don't find a system that works like this, it's just going to become a carbon tax. So it's much better for the farmer to get paid for the good work, instead of taxing everybody, which includes the farmer."** — flips the political-skepticism objection.
8. **"AgriProve also functions as kind of a risk buffer. The only thing the farmer pays is the upfront sampling cost."** — names the asymmetric-risk reality in one line.
9. **"The beautiful thing about AgriProve is that we let you guys farm the way you think you should farm. We're not an agronomy service."** — locks down the agnostic-on-practices positioning.
10. **"If our management and our production and our profitability are all growing, then by definition our carbon should be growing as well. You can't decrease soil health for 30 years and expect everything to go up."** — reframes carbon as a derivative of good management, not a separate project.
11. **"The future of beef is going to look like the past 50 years of wine. Instead of just red or white, you'll want from this vineyard, this year."** — future-orientation hook that gets operators excited about provenance.
12. **"With these kind of numbers for 30 years, haven't been getting paid for that. And you should have."** — the moment when an existing-good-operator realises they've been leaving money on the table.
13. **"The people who figure out how to use the land the best will be the people who end up with all the land."** — long-arc legacy hook.
14. **"I would not recommend it. It's like — if you want to do that, you might as well do your own taxes."** — neutralises the DIY objection.
15. **"We're now the most audited company for soil carbon in Australia. ISO 9001 certification."** — the trust/track-record hook.
16. **"It becomes interestingly enough like a land acquisition tool. A financial derivative of productivity."** — reframes carbon for buyers/aggregators.
17. **"Now we can run the satellite over every month. The second we see carbon levels are up, that triggers sampling, so you never leave any money on the table."** — explains the methodology upgrade without jargon.
18. **"Down the line when Woolworths and Coles have to account for their entire supply chain down to the farm — if you're sitting there holding those ACCUs, they'll have to buy them at some point."** — Scope-3 inevitability hook for sophisticated operators.
19. **"Your flat country can go up and your hill country goes backwards. If they're in the one project, you went up by three, down by three — you get zero. So we register them as two projects. We pick up the cost."** — methodology + customer-aligned-incentive in one move.
20. **"Then we kick off the excruciating process that you don't have to handle at all."** — sequencing the funnel while reassuring on regulator burden.
21. **"Remember, I'm just the Grazier who's come in and sort of observing from the outside."** — the de-positioning move; he's not the closer, AgriProve's machine is.
22. **"It's the only thing that goes straight to your bottom line — not a cost item on your balance sheet."** — ACCU framing for financially-literate operators.

## Patterns in Hobbs's approach

### Sequence
He almost never opens with carbon. The recon phase is long and substantive — he asks about the operation, the soils, the genetics, the rotation, the family history. Once the operator has fully described their world, he transitions with a question that surfaces an opportunity: "what do you know about carbon?" or "let me just talk first about what could possibly make you guys money." The carbon pitch lands on already-warm ground because the operator has just spent 30-60 minutes explaining everything good they're doing.

### Signature moves

1. **De-positioning ("I'm just the Grazier")** — used in 4 of 6 visits. Strips the salesperson dynamic. Makes AgriProve's back-office machine the protagonist.
2. **Math on hectares, live** — never lets the conversation stay abstract. Pulls out the calculator, uses their actual hectare count, current spot price, 3 ACCUs/ha, 75% share. Always lands as a tangible number.
3. **Case-study cheques** — has 3 specific cheque examples memorised ([Queensland NRM] $60k → $500k; 83-ha → $45k cheque; 1000-ha → ~$14k baseline cap). Uses them as proof of return, not theory.
4. **Reduces the contract to two clauses** — every time the 25-year question comes up: "make a commitment to be better, make a commitment to keep your land in the agricultural system for 25 years." Removes the bureaucratic dread.
5. **Refuses to play agronomist** — when asked "what should we do to increase carbon?" he stays in lane: "we let you farm how you think you should farm." Reinforces the agnostic positioning and protects the customer relationship from feeling like a sale.
6. **Names what AgriProve absorbs** — the risk-buffer line and the audit-machine line do parallel work: they explain why the 25% success fee is fair and why the operator's downside is bounded.
7. **Validates the cynic** — when operators push back ("why pay for what we'd do anyway?", "doesn't seem to add up"), he praises the question ("you're poking the argument at its weakest point — that's a good idea"). Disarms without conceding. Doesn't always convert (visit 5), but never escalates.
8. **Big macro framing for sophisticated operators** — Scope 3 supply chain, beef-as-wine provenance, digital twins for bankability, soil-carbon-as-land-acquisition-derivative. Used selectively with operators who have a strategic mindset (visits 1, 3, 4).
9. **Vulnerability as trust device** — "I'm an American just trying to figure out what's going on here" / "I'm just learning under the hood." Counter-intuitively builds credibility because he's not pretending to be the regulator.
10. **Sequenced next step** — always closes by naming the next concrete low-commitment action: HORIZON Snapshot first, then 1hr land-management call with Ben, then optional registration. Never asks for commitment in the room.

### Rapport-build patterns (compressed)

- Always notes connections to Australian-American crossings (his Texas/ranching background, "we were in California when our first kid was born", his Magaret/French name pronunciation).
- References specific Australian agricultural figures by name when the operator name-drops (Mark Lucas, Will Donovan, Wilmot/Alistair McLeod, Gabe Brown, Elaine Ingham) — signals he's in the conversation, not adjacent to it.
- When operators show him their land, he asks genuinely good operator questions (rotation logic, weaning timing, EBV vs phenotype). The carbon pitch lands because they've already accepted him as a peer-operator.

## Limitations / gaps

1. **Speaker labels reset per visit.** Hobbs is sometimes Speaker 1 (visit 5, 6), sometimes Speaker 2 (visit 1), sometimes Speaker 6 (visit 3), and in visit 3 there's clearly a second AgriProve voice (likely Ben Newey based on methodology specificity) labelled Speaker 1 — Hobbs is Speaker 6 in that visit. Visits 3+4 may overlap or be one extended visit-day across multiple recording segments — they share Sam/Ryland Angus context but the otter.ai markers separate them. I treated them as two visits but the boundary is fuzzy.

2. **Visit 5 (Monaro) is shorter and more ambiguous.** The recording cuts off into food/dinner chat. Pitch was partial and Hobbs didn't fully close on the cynic-mode pushback. Marked outcome as neutral and confidence on some distillates as moderate.

3. **Visit dates not in transcript.** All dates marked "unknown". Cross-reference against Outlook calendar / Granola if needed for downstream prioritisation.

4. **Regions PII-generalised.** Where Hobbs named specific towns/regions (Hinty, Holbrook, Tumut, Wagga, Monaro/Bombala), I generalised to NRM clusters. Specific case-study locations (Queensland projects) abstracted to "[Queensland NRM region]".

5. **Internal AgriProve sessions excluded** (4 segments, lines 1844-2143, 2143-2582, 6441-6608, plus the wrap-up at 1844). These contain valuable strategy and pricing info (commercial funding model with corporate carbon, board-prep narrative, Storm Boy ops) but are not farm visits and don't belong in this Pass 0 cache. They may warrant separate processing for internal strategy/learnings.

6. **No customer-position quotes captured verbatim** per PII rules. All customer positions are paraphrased and PII-stripped.

7. **Confidence calibration.** "High" confidence is used when Hobbs's framing is clearly captured and the customer reaction is observable in the transcript. "Moderate" is used when transcript audio quality (per otter.ai limits) leaves attribution ambiguous or when the customer reaction is unclear. "Low" was not used — borderline content was either elevated to moderate or omitted.
